html:
The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or Seven Council Fires, are the peoples better known as the Sioux. They are the Lakota of the west, the Dakota of the east, among them the Mdewakanton, Wahpeton, Wahpekute and Sisseton, and the Yankton and Yanktonai in between. They speak dialects of one Siouan language.

Around 1492 their ancestors lived in the woodlands and prairies of today's Minnesota, hunting, fishing, gathering wild rice and growing some crops. In the 1700s many bands moved west onto the plains. With horses the Lakota became mounted bison hunters and the strongest power on the northern plains, taking the Black Hills from other peoples.

The 1800s brought war with the United States. The Dakota fought the Dakota War of 1862 in Minnesota, after which 38 Dakota men were hanged. The Lakota won the right to the Black Hills in the Fort Laramie treaty of 1868, then lost them after gold was found. They defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876 but were forced onto reservations. The Wounded Knee Massacre of 1890 closed the wars.

Their descendants live on reservations in the Dakotas, Minnesota, Nebraska and Montana, and in Canada. In 2016 protests at Standing Rock against an oil pipeline drew wide attention.
